comment: Regression bounds for scripts/benchmark-sync.mjs. A baseline is the number a
clean run produced on the machine named in `measuredOn`; the policy factors turn
each one into a floor (throughput) or a ceiling (time, memory). Re-measure with
the move in the pull request -- these are not knobs to turn until CI is green.
The published baseline table lives in docs/benchmarks.md.

calibrationComment: "applied" scales throughput and elapsed checks by the reference workload;
"diagnostic" measures and reports it but does not let it decide. It is
diagnostic because two ubuntu-latest runners disagreed about which of them was
faster depending on the phase -- the reference said the 6973P-C was 1.29x
quicker while cold_sync said the 8573C was 1.32x quicker -- so no single scalar
can normalize all five phases. Scaling by it failed an entirely healthy run
(PR #202, job 106023782674). The 2x and 1.5x margins are the contention
allowance; a second, sometimes anti-correlated corrector on top made the gate
worse. Flip this to "applied" to restore the previous behaviour.
offClassComment: What happens on a runner whose CPU is not in `measuredOn.cpusSeen`. The bounds
are widened -- never tightened, never past `offClassCalibrationCap`. A bound
derived from a stored baseline is widened by the calibration ratio clamped to
[1, cap]; an elapsed ceiling that comes from an absolute floor is widened by the
full cap and a breach inside that widening is advisory rather than fatal, because
such a floor is a runner-noise allowance measured on the baseline class and the
calibration is a CPU-speed reading that does not describe walk-and-stat jitter.
peakRssBytes is never widened. On the baseline class none of this applies. See
docs/benchmarks.md, 'A runner the baselines were never measured on'.
absoluteFloorsComment: A ceiling derived from a very small baseline measures the runner, not the
code. These floors raise such a ceiling and never lower one. On the tiny PR
store the peak-RSS check is therefore a blow-up guard -- it catches 'the whole
store is now buffered in memory', not a 1.5x drift. The proportional rule
bites on the `full` profile, whose store is two orders of magnitude larger.
absoluteFloorsByPhaseComment: Some tiny elapsed-time phases need a higher final ceiling than the metric-wide
floor because observed runner jitter on github-hosted ubuntu-latest is already
above 2x their stored baseline. Keep these phase-scoped so other elapsed checks
unchanged_sync went 120 -> 140 in #198, which makes Cursor an event-level
source. The phase got slower because the store got bigger, not because a no-op
tick got worse: the synthetic store's Cursor transcripts now yield 192
session_events rows that no release before it stored, so the database grows
~0.3 MiB and an unchanged tick reads ~0.4 MiB more of it. Measured on one
machine across four commits -- old main ~100ms, main+#196 ~102ms, #198 ~112ms --
and on a github-hosted ubuntu-latest (AMD EPYC 7763) the PR head measured
125.3ms against the old 120 ceiling. 120 was itself set against ~113ms of
healthy observed runs, about 6% of headroom; 140 keeps ~12% over the 125.3ms
worst case seen on the slowest CPU in the pool. The stored ci-debug baseline
(51ms) is untouched and still needs a re-measure on the gate's machine class.

ci-debug.description: Fast PR gate: an unoptimized build against a small synthetic store, sized to keep the whole gate inside 60 s on a 4-core runner. Baselines are the worst value each metric took across the observed ubuntu-latest CPUs, so both pass with the issue's 2x/1.5x factors and neither CPU sets a bar the other cannot clear.

measuredOn.machineClass: github-hosted ubuntu-latest, 4 cores, 15.6 GiB, Node 20, debug build
measuredOn.rule: each baseline is the worse of the two runs -- lowest throughput, longest time, largest RSS -- rounded away from the bound (floors down, ceilings up) so that rounding cannot make a limit stricter than the run it came from, and a bound set by one CPU cannot fail the other
measuredOn.supersedes: baselines measured on an Intel Xeon 2.80GHz development box at 2a1e81a. They failed the gate on a healthy runner because that machine is not in the pool the gate runs on, and the calibration factor that was supposed to bridge the difference is anti-correlated with cold_sync across these CPUs.

full.description: Release-build matrix run by .github/workflows/benchmark-sync.yml on workflow_dispatch. Not a PR gate: it has no stored baselines, it publishes numbers.
